author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

text:
In the AI era, what is knowledge?

The definition of knowledge evolves alongside technological development. In ancient times, before the invention of writing, knowledge existed within the oral traditions of tribes; a person possessed only as much knowledge as they could hold in their memory. Later, writing was invented, but copying books remained expensive. While the importance of pure memory declined slightly, reading and writing became the sole methods for transmitting knowledge. Consequently, the ability to recite the contents of books became the universal standard for representing knowledge.

With the invention of the printing press, books became popularized, and universities and libraries were established. Mere rote memory no longer represented knowledge; it became little more than a parlor trick for entertainment. The representative power of knowledge in that era shifted to the ability to organize, synthesize, and summarize large volumes of books and text. Through the evolution of the Internet and Google, the amount of data a person could master and digest grew increasingly abundant. However, this did not shake the definition of knowledge established in the print era; it only deepened its influence.

However, the sudden emergence of ChatGPT has brought about earth-shattering changes in just three short years. Resource organization and curation that once took a team of people months to complete can now be easily finished by AI in ten minutes. The role of a mere "knowledge porter" is no longer valuable; some academic journals have even banned the publication of survey-style papers because they are simply too easy to mass-produce now. So, in the era of AI, what constitutes knowledge?

Knowledge in itself is static; applying knowledge to solve the difficulties we face is what makes it alive. AI can answer any of our questions, but ultimately, it is still up to us to decide whether or not to trust the answer it provides. This cycle has not changed since the beginning of time. In ancient times, we chose whether to listen to the wisdom of our elders; more recently, we learned that blind faith in books is worse than having no books at all; and in the past few years, we learned that even the almighty Google makes mistakes.

Technology has merely accelerated the process of querying existing knowledge, allowing us to quickly verify the authenticity of answers. AI has not changed the definition of knowledge; rather, it has unveiled its most primitive and original face: Knowledge has always been about making the right decisions.
